title: Econ walkthrough — prefetch & batching roadmap w/ Verdemar Technologies
summary: Redwood team ran a focused Optimize walkthrough covering prefix/KV prefetch recommendations, batching heuristics and a cost-simulation using the console. Verdemar is evaluating a hybrid hosted + private deployment for latency sensitive endpoints; main goals were to understand cost tradeoffs, expected latency impact, and what data/security controls are needed for a pilot.
topics: latency SLO impact and tail latency
transcript: [00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. We're gonna run through an Optimize walkthrough — mostly prefix and KV prefetch, and then show the cost sim in the console. Maya, Ibrahim, Tom — can you hear us ok?

[00:14] Maya (Verdemar): Yeah good, can hear you. Thanks, uh, for putting this together. We ran the quick questionnaire — our main, main constraints are sub-200ms p95 for our chat assistant, and we'd like to not blow our budget.
[00:29] Alex: Perfect. Quick intros: Samir will do the deep dive on the caching strategy and cost model, I'll steer the console demo and next steps. Sound good?

[00:42] Samir (Redwood SE): Yup — I pulled a couple of traces from your sample logs that you shared, and modeled a mixed workload: 60% short queries (~30-40 tokens) and 40% long form (~200 tokens) with session affinity. We'll show a few knobs — prefetch horizon, KV TTL, batch timeout and max batch size — and the simulated cost outcomes.

[01:05] Tom (SRE): Quick Q before we go deep: sensitive PII flows through some sessions. We plan to keep keys in our KMS and want guaranteed no-model-logging for private endpoints. How does that affect caching?

[01:20] Samir: Good question. Short answer: caching (prefix or KV) is independent of model logging; you can disable transcript retention and use customer-managed KMS. For private deployments we support HSM/KMS integrations and an audit log export; that will be in the security docs we'll share. But operationally, TTLs and eviction policies still apply — if you need ephemeral-only, set very short TTLs or disable persistent KV.
[01:45] Ibrahim (CTO): So with KMS and no retention, can we still do prefix caching across requests? We don't want cross-session data leakage.

[01:56] Samir: Yes — prefix caching can be scoped per-session or per-user key. We typically recommend session-scoped prefix cache for chat since it preserves privacy boundaries. You can also enable encryption at rest via your KMS key and RBAC to limit which Redwood service accounts can read the cache. There's a tradeoff: broader scope increases hit-rate and savings but requires stricter controls.
[02:20] [Speaker 2 — minor glitch]: (inaudible) — sorry, dropped for a sec.
[02:28] Alex: No worries. Ok Samir, can you show the first scenario — aggressive prefetch vs conservative?

[02:35] Samir: Sure. In the console I'm loading Verdemar test workload. Scenario A: lookahead prefetch 128 tokens, KV TTL 24h, batch max 64, batch timeout 25ms. Scenario B: prefetch 32 tokens, TTL 5m, batch max 16, timeout 50ms. The cost sim shows scenario A reduces per-token unit cost by ~28% for your workload but increases median latency ~15ms and tightens tail depending on concurrency. I'll start the sim...
[03:10] [00:03:10] — console clicks —

[03:18] Samir: Here are the numbers — baseline (no prefetch/cache) estimates $X per 1M tokens, p95 190ms. Scenario A ~ $0.72X, p95 205ms. Scenario B ~ $0.92X, p95 195ms. So you can see the delta. Note these are model-variant aware — we assume running the 7B quantized variant the whole time; switching to a slower higher-quality variant changes the absolute numbers.

[03:52] Maya: That gap looks good. For the latency, p95 205ms still under our 200ms target for some endpoints, it's close, but some real traffic spikes might push it over. Is there a way to keep savings but avoid p95 regressions?

[04:06] Samir: Yes — two levers: dynamic routing and hybrid prefetch. Use small prefetch horizon for low-latency routes and larger prefetch for batchy background requests. Also, advanced batching: sticky sessions + concurrency shaping so that low-latency users hit freshly primed workers with reserved capacity. That keeps their p95 lower while overall throughput benefits.
[04:35] Tom: You mentioned reserved capacity — would that be Redwood Dedicated? We're thinking hosted for now but may reserve a pool for the critical route.

[04:45] Alex: Exactly. Hosted API can get you started, Optimize recommendations still apply. Dedicated gives more predictable tail latency because you can pin workers and avoid noisy neighbors. There's also Private for VPC if you want KMS inside your VPC and strict egress controls.
[04:59] Ibrahim: Cost model — can we plug in our actual cloud-GPU price? We need end-to-end TCO to compare against running in-house.

[05:09] Samir: Yep — in the console you can override infra unit cost and attach a custom GPU price, as well as include our per-token hosted fee or exclude it for a Private deployment. I put in your rough EC2 spot vs reserved numbers and it adjusted the sim — when you account for ops overhead, the Redwood hybrid tends to be cheaper for your traffic profile, but we can export the CSV for your finance team to model. I'll export and send it.
[05:35] Maya: Nice. Can you walk through how KV TTL interacts with prefix prefetch? We worry about TTL causing stale context.

[05:44] Samir: TTL affects the lifetime of the cached KV entries; prefix prefetch is often a one-shot replication of likely continuations into KV. For chat you want per-session prefix cache with TTL aligned to session timeout (e.g., 30–60 min) unless the application requires longer memory. If your app needs persistent memory, you store summaries outside the KV with explicit retention policies. The Optimize console recommends TTL based on session length distribution it infers from logs.
[06:12] [06:12] Maya: There's a lot of vocabulary here — prefix, KV, lookahead, sessionization — can you give a one-line mapping for our infra team?

[06:20] Samir: Sure. Prefix cache stores the initial tokens or common completions so the model doesn't recompute them; KV cache stores key/value attention state to skip recomputing earlier layers for long contexts; lookahead prefetch asks the runtime to compute likely next KV states ahead of time. Put simply: prefix reduces tokens generated, KV reduces compute for repeated contexts.
[06:44] Tom: Any gotchas when we enable KV for mixed-length workloads? We saw strange latency spikes in a PoC last year.

[06:53] Samir: Spikes usually come from large KV loads at high concurrency — that’s why batching, sticky session routing, and worker sizing matter. The runtime supports continuous batching and KV sharding; the console suggests shard sizes based on observed session length percentiles. Also watch memory pressures — quantized model variants affect KV memory footprint. We'll include mem estimates in the export.

[07:20] [07:20] Alex: Quick demo of the Optimize recommendation card — note how it calls out savings, expected p50/p95 deltas, and the recommended rollout policy (canary 5%, then 25%). I'll flip to the rollout UI.

[07:38] [clicks] Samir: The rollout policy can also auto-fallback to baseline model if latency or error rate exceeds thresholds. For example, if p95 climbs >20% or error rate >0.5% we auto-fallback. That keeps customer-facing endpoints safe while you experiment.
[07:55] Ibrahim: For our compliance team, we need audit logs for who changed TTLs and rollouts, plus SSO. Do you provide immutable logs?

[08:05] Alex: Yes — audit trails and change history are part of Redwood Private and Dedicated with extended retention as an add-on. SSO (SAML/SCIM) and RBAC are standard on enterprise plans. We'll attach the SOC2 / ISO docs.
[08:18] Maya: Could you show a concrete example — like how many tokens saved per session if we prefetch N tokens?

[08:26] Samir: I ran a sample on your dataset: average tokens generated per session baseline 420. With a 64-token prefetch and good hit-rate the generated tokens drop to ~310 on average — roughly 26% reduction. But if your user base prefers long multi-turn generative sessions the marginal returns drop. The console graphs the diminishing returns so you can pick the knee of the curve.
[08:56] Tom: And does prefetch increase cold-start memory? We were constrained on our spot instances.

[09:03] Samir: Prefetch increases temporary memory per worker but the main pressure is persistent KV size and shard count. For spot instances, we recommend smaller shard sizes and a conservative prefetch horizon. There's a recommended profile labeled 'spot-friendly' in the Optimize console.
[09:23] [09:23] Maya: Could you run a 'what-if' showing a mid-tier lane where we set reserved capacity for 10% of traffic?

[09:30] Alex: Yeah, I'll toggle reserved capacity to 10% and rerun. — Ok rerun complete. Results: reserved pool reduces the p95 for the reserved route to 170ms while overall p95 (global) stays ~200ms; cost increases by ~8% due to idle reserved capacity but it flattens tail spikes. This is the classic latency vs cost tradeoff.
[10:02] Ibrahim: Is there a recommended rollout cadence? We run an internal canary program already.

[10:09] Samir: We recommend mirror testing, then a 1% canary in production, 5% after 24–48h if metrics look good, then 25%. The console automates metric checks and can automatically rollback. We'll show you the default thresholds and how to tweak them for your KPIs.
[10:29] Tom: A surprise question — tokenization differences. Our pre-tokenization pipeline sometimes strips emojis and that messes up prefix matches. Any support?

[10:38] Samir: Prefix hits depend on deterministic tokenization. We support custom tokenizers and can align prefix logic to your pipeline. If emoji stripping is needed, do it consistently pre-insert into session context so the cache keys match. We'll flag that in the integration notes.
[10:56] Maya: Can you show the CSV export with cost breakdown so our finance team can plug it into their model?
[11:03] Alex: Exporting now... done, sent link in chat. It has rows per scenario, cost per 100k tokens, inferred GPU-hours, and recommended batch sizes.
[11:12] [11:12] Maya: Got it. I see one scenario with a big drop but the p95 is 220ms — not acceptable. How do we tune to keep p95 under 200 and still save >15%?

[11:22] Samir: The console suggests combination: small prefetch + KV for mid-turn reuse + reserved capacity for 10% of traffic + a max batch size cap of 32. That combo gives ~16–18% savings while keeping p95 ~195ms in the sim.
[11:44] Ibrahim: Any architecture docs for hybrid routing? Our infra team wants a diagram for sticky sessions + reserved pool + fallback.

[11:52] Alex: We'll attach the architecture diagram and the sample routing policy JSON. It shows route priorities: 1) reserved pool by route tag, 2) regional fallback, 3) model-variant downgrade. We'll also include sample autoscaling policies tuned for your concurrency distribution.
[12:12] Tom: For the pilot, we'd like a small PoC for a single route for 2 weeks. Can we get a sandbox with 100k monthly token allowance to run it?
[12:22] Alex: Yes — we can spin a sandbox pilot with a shared sandbox project, provide a guide, and an engineer to help with instrumentation. We'll propose an SOW for the pilot.
[12:33] Maya: Awesome. A few nitty-gritty: Does Optimize persist our workload traces in Redwood? We prefer only aggregated metrics stored.

[12:41] Samir: By default we store aggregated telemetry. Raw payloads and transcripts are opt-in; for Private deployments you can disable all raw retention. We'll specify the default retention windows in the security doc.

[13:02] Alex: Ok two quick advanced items: 1) adaptive batching — runtime will increase batch timeout under load to improve batch efficiency while honoring latency SLOs; 2) lookahead prefetch policy can be ML-driven — it learns which tokens to prefetch to maximize hit-rate. Both are opt-in. Want a quick peek?
[13:21] Maya: Yes please the ML-driven lookahead sounds promising. How safe is it?

[13:27] Samir: It starts conservatively and you can enable progressively. It only prefetches internal KV states, not user-provided secrets, and adheres to your scoping. We monitor drift in hit-rate and expose a confidence score. You can gate it behind the canary rollout.
[13:45] Tom: Any specific SLO recommendations for retries and fallback? We run a tight retry budget to avoid duplicates.

[13:53] Samir: Keep retry budget small for interactive routes; prefer instant fallback to baseline model or a cached short-form response. The console can mark a route as 'no-retry' to prevent duplicate costs. We'll show that in the policy export.
[14:12] Ibrahim: Great. Can you summarize the recommended pilot config?

[14:17] Alex: Pilot config (in plain English): 1) Use hosted sandbox with reserved pool 10% for critical route; 2) enable session-scoped prefix cache with 30m TTL; 3) set prefetch horizon 32 tokens initially; 4) batch cap 32, timeout 30ms; 5) enable canary rollout 1% -> 5% -> 25% with auto-fallback; 6) disable transcript retention and use customer KMS. We'll include exact config JSON.
[14:46] Maya: Sounds good. Can we have the Redwood SE join our infra sync next Wednesday?
14:52] Alex: Samir can join — we'll propose times.
[14:56] Samir: I'll take the action items on the integration checklist and the CSV export follow-up.
[15:03] [15:03] Maya: Okay appreciate it, this was helpful. One more small ask — can we get a rough timeline for Dedicated if pilot goes well?
[15:12] Alex: Dedicated procurement usually runs 6–8 weeks from signed contract to capacity, less if you're using our marketplace flow. We'll give a ramp plan.
[15:24] Ibrahim: Thanks everyone.
[15:28] Alex: Quick recap and next steps coming up in chat. We'll close in a minute.
[15:32] [15:32] — meeting wrap —

Share exported cost CSV and console scenario link (Samir)
Schedule SE integration sync next Wednesday (Samir + Verdemar infra)
